definition: The study and design of how people interact with computers, so technology is useful, usable and safe.
How easily and efficiently people can use a product to reach their goals, and how satisfied they are doing it.
The whole experience a person has with a product: how it works, how it feels and how it fits their needs.
A design process that keeps users' needs, goals and limits at the center of every stage, with repeated testing.
A human-centered problem-solving approach: Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype and Test, repeated as needed.
A chart of what a user says, thinks, does and feels, used to build a shared understanding of them.
A fictional but research-based user profile with goals, needs and frustrations that represents a user group.
A visual timeline of the steps, touchpoints and emotions a user goes through to reach a goal.
A moment in the user's journey where they feel frustrated, confused or blocked.
A user's own idea of how a system works, which shapes what they expect it to do.
The mental effort needed to use an interface. Good design keeps it low by reducing what users must remember.
A property of an object that suggests how it can be used, like a button that looks pressable.
A visible cue that shows where or how to act, such as a label, icon or arrow.
The system's response to an action, such as a spinner, sound or message, so users know what happened.
The relationship between controls and their effects; natural mapping makes it obvious which control does what.
Limits that prevent wrong actions, like greying out a button until a form is complete.
Using the same patterns, words and styles throughout, so users can reuse what they already learned.
Don Norman's seven-stage action cycle, split into Execution (doing) and Evaluation (checking the result).
The gap between what a user wants to do and the actions the system allows.
The gap between the system's state and the user's understanding of whether their action worked.
A cognitive model that breaks a task into Goals, Operators, Methods and Selection rules to predict user performance.
A GOMS variant that predicts task time by adding up standard times for keystrokes, pointing and thinking.
The time to reach a target depends on its distance and size: bigger and closer targets are faster to hit.
The more choices people have, the longer it takes them to decide.
Rules for how people group what they see: proximity, similarity, closure, continuity and figure-ground.
Jakob Nielsen's ten rules of thumb for usable interfaces, such as visibility of system status and error prevention.
An expert review that checks an interface against a set of usability heuristics.
A simple layout of a screen that shows structure and content placement without visual styling.
A rough, quick model (paper sketches or simple wireframes) used to test ideas early and cheaply.
A detailed, interactive model that looks and behaves close to the final product.
Watching real users try tasks with a product to find problems and improve the design.
A testing method where users say what they are thinking while they use a product.
Comparing two versions of a design with real users to see which one performs better.
Designing so people with disabilities can perceive, understand, navigate and use a product.
The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, built on four principles: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust.
Tools that help people with disabilities use computers, such as screen readers, magnifiers and switch controls.
Designing for the full range of human diversity, including ability, language, culture and age.
Deceptive design tricks that push users into actions they did not intend, like hidden costs or forced sign-ups.
A framework that compares cultures on dimensions such as power distance and individualism, used in global design.
Don Norman's idea that design affects people on three levels: visceral (looks), behavioral (use) and reflective (meaning).
An interface people use through natural language, such as a chatbot.
An interface controlled by speech, like a smart speaker assistant.
Adds digital content on top of the real world, usually through a phone camera or glasses.
A fully digital, immersive environment experienced through a headset.
An interface where people control digital information by handling physical objects.
Computing built into everyday objects and spaces so it works in the background, anywhere.
A system's ability to sense its situation (location, time, activity) and adapt to it.
